title: Investor Types and Their Liabilities
text: Investor Types and Their Liabilities 3 Della Croce, R. (2012), OECD Working Paper 29, page 7; Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Review of Financial Studies 34(8), pages 3888 and 3909. title: Allocations Differ Widely across Pension Funds
text: Allocations Differ Widely across Pension Funds 4 Headline: 28 large funds held 2.9 per cent of their assets in infrastructure in 2010, mostly as unlisted equity Spread: from 15.5 per cent at OMERS to 0.3 per cent at ABP Route: of the unlisted equity, USD 30.9 billion was direct and USD 7.0 billion through funds Caution: 2010 data for large funds; listed holdings sit inside equity allocations Source: Della Croce, R. (2012), Trends in large pension fund investment in infrastructure, OECD Working Papers on Finance, Insurance and Private Pensions No. 29, Table 5 (page 23) and pages 4 and 8.

title: Routes Used by Institutional Investors
text: Routes Used by Institutional Investors 5 Closed funds: 538 funds are the main route for most investors Direct deals: open to a few deep-pocketed investors, with the top 20 making 55 per cent of them By investor type: sovereign funds and government agencies invest directly; endowments and private pension funds use funds Reading: the shares compare investor-fund with investor-deal observations, not dollars Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Review of Financial Studies 34(8), Figure 1 and footnotes 2 and 6 (pages 3882 and 3888). Shares are the author's arithmetic on investor-fund (closed funds) and investor-deal (direct) observations.

title: Funding the Data Centre
text: Funding the Data Centre 6 Scale: 188 GW and about US$9 trillion over 2025 to 2032, 3.22 per cent of GDP a year Cost: about US$41 million a megawatt: 11 for the building, 2 for power, 28 for chips and network The gap: hyperscaler capex exceeds operating cash flow for the first time in 2026 The response: leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit and securitisation Van Nieuwerburgh, S. (2026), Financing the AI Buildout, NBER Working Paper 35865, Figure 1 and pages 2 to 8. Capex excludes data centres the hyperscalers lease; 2026 combines results, guidance and analysts' estimates.

title: The Capital Stack of a Data Centre
text: The Capital Stack of a Data Centre 7 Note: Hyperion (Meta and Blue Owl, 2025): about US$30 billion; 80 per cent of the equity sold for about US$2.5 billion; US$27 billion of debt rated A+, about 90 per cent of asset value, debt service cover 1.12, yield 6.58 per cent. Van Nieuwerburgh, S. (2026), Financing the AI Buildout, NBER Working Paper 35865, pages 2 and 6–10. Hyperion figures are the paper's and are to be verified against the rating agency report before publication. Layer Who supplies it Instrument What it is exposed to Tenant Investment-grade hyperscalers Internal cash flow, corporate debt, leases, guarantees Demand for compute Third-party equity Developers, infrastructure funds, REITs, private equity Equity in vehicles and joint ventures Utilisation and residual value Project debt Banks and private credit funds Mortgage loans, syndicated lines, private credit Tenant credit and asset value Structured finance Bond and securitisation investors Bonds from special-purpose vehicles backed by leases Tenant concentration IT equipment Lessors and asset-backed investors Leases and asset-backed securities Obsolescence

title: The Fund as the Vehicle
text: The Fund as the Vehicle 8 The structure: a limited partnership raised for 10 to 12 years, with capital called, invested and returned When the money moves: calls early, distributions late, and a J-curve between them Who is paid for what: a fixed fee and a share of the profit that behaves like an option What the investor needs: an asset that moves with its liabilities, at a cost in liquidity Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Review of Financial Studies 34(8), page 3888; Metrick and Yasuda (2007), Wharton Rodney L. White Center Working Paper 17-07, page 2.

title: Takahashi and Alexander (2002): Cash Flows
text: Takahashi and Alexander (2002): Cash Flows 9 Calls: a time-varying share of the commitment not yet called Distributions: a time-varying share of the grown asset value, never below the yield Value: last year's value grown at G, plus calls, less distributions Inputs: commitment, life, rate of contribution, bow factor, growth and yield Takahashi, D. and Alexander, S. (2002), Illiquid alternative asset fund modeling, Journal of Portfolio Management 28(2), 90–100, as stated in Karatas, Klinkert and Hirsa (2021), arXiv 2108.02853, page 3.

title: The J-Curve of a Ten-Year Fund
text: The J-Curve of a Ten-Year Fund 10 Calls come first: the investor is a net payer for the first years The J: the deepest cumulative outlay is about three quarters of the commitment, in year 4 Recovery: the cumulative flow turns positive in year 8 at 9 per cent net growth Programme: annual commitments take years to build a stable portfolio Author's calculation from the Takahashi and Alexander (2002) model as stated in Karatas, Klinkert and Hirsa (2021), arXiv 2108.02853, page 3; illustrative inputs (models_w3.py).

title: Metrick and Yasuda (2010): Fees as Claims
text: Metrick and Yasuda (2010): Fees as Claims 11 Fixed claim: the management fee is paid whatever the fund earns Variable claim: carried interest is a fraction of the profit and has the shape of a call option Equilibrium: limited partners must earn their cost of capital after the manager is paid Result: about 60 per cent of expected manager revenue is fixed Metrick, A. and Yasuda, A. (2010), The economics of private equity funds, Review of Financial Studies 23(6), 2303–2341; Wharton Rodney L. White Center Working Paper 17-07 (2007), abstract and pages 2, 11–12 and 16.

title: The Value of Fixed and Variable Fees
text: The Value of Fixed and Variable Fees 12 The shape: carry pays nothing below the hurdle, then rises with proceeds The claim gains from risk: its value rises with volatility, as an option does Default terms: fees 12.2 and carry 5.4 per 100 committed, a fixed share of 69 per cent The price: the fund must beat its investable capital by about 1.9 per cent a year Author's calculation after Metrick and Yasuda (2010): carry as a call option on a single exit, closed form (models_w3.py); 1.5% fee, 4% risk-free rate, 10 years. Illustrative.

title: Keel and Müller (1995): Assets against Liabilities
text: Keel and Müller (1995): Assets against Liabilities 13 The problem: maximise expected surplus return less half its variance, where surplus is assets less liabilities The result: the liability shifts the minimum-risk portfolio, whatever the investor's risk tolerance The test: an asset earns its place by its correlation with the liability, not only by its own risk The caveat: one period, no illiquidity, and the correlation is an assumption Keel, A. and Müller, H. H. (1995), Efficient portfolios in the asset liability context, ASTIN Bulletin 25(1), 33–48, pages 33–39; after Sharpe, W. F. and Tint, L. G. (1990), Journal of Portfolio Management 16(2), 5–10.

title: Hedging the Liability with Real Assets
text: Hedging the Liability with Real Assets 14 Hedge portfolio: counting the liability moves the minimum-risk mix from 36 to 31 per cent infrastructure, and shorts equities Chosen portfolio: at a risk tolerance of 0.2, 53 per cent infrastructure and 45 per cent gilts The link matters: the weight runs from 2 to 84 per cent as the correlation with the liability rises from 0 to 0.9 Illiquidity: the cost the asset can bear is 2.6 per cent a year at the default settings Author's calculation after Keel and Müller (1995), ASTIN Bulletin 25(1), pages 35–39 (models_w3.py); illustrative returns, volatilities and correlations; risk tolerance 0.2, funding ratio 1.

title: Three Models of the Fund Compared
text: Three Models of the Fund Compared 15 Karatas, Klinkert and Hirsa (2021), page 3; Metrick and Yasuda (2007), abstract and page 16; Keel and Müller (1995), pages 38–39; Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), pages 3882–3883. Model Explains Prediction Evidence and limit Takahashi and Alexander (2002) When the money moves Calls early, returns late: a J-curve and a mid-life exposure peak Standard planning tool; deterministic, silent on fees and return Metrick and Yasuda (2010) Who is paid for what Carry is an option, worth more with risk; most revenue is fixed 238 funds, about 60 per cent fixed; one investor's data Keel and Müller (1995) What the investor needs An asset earns its place by its link to the liability Theory; one period; funds look like other private funds

title: Risk and Return of Unlisted Infrastructure Funds
text: Risk and Return of Unlisted Infrastructure Funds 16 Average: a public market equivalent of 0.93, below buyout, venture capital and real estate Risk-adjusted: a loss of 0.257 per dollar committed, comparable to venture capital Dispersion: 0.31, similar to buyout and real estate, below venture capital Leverage: the median infrastructure deal is financed 66 per cent by debt Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Review of Financial Studies 34(8), Table 6 (page 3908) and pages 3882–3883 and 3909. GPME from Korteweg and Nagel's method; funds raised 2002–2018.

title: Exits, Cash Flows and Investor Type
text: Exits, Cash Flows and Investor Type 17 Closed funds are paid to exit quickly, and public investors in them earn less, after controlling for deal stage, region and industry. Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Review of Financial Studies 34(8), Table 4 (page 3899), Table 8 (page 3915) and pages 3883–3884. Association with performance Public market equivalent Net IRR, percentage points Multiple of invested capital 10 percentage points more of deals exited in years 0 to 5 +0.085 +2.575 +0.079 A public investor, compared with a private investor −0.026 −1.810 −0.038

title: Default and Recovery in Project Finance Loans
text: Default and Recovery in Project Finance Loans 18 Default: 5.0 per cent of project loans default within ten years on the Basel definition, 3.2 per cent on Moody's Recovery: the average recovery is 81.5 per cent, and the median is 100 per cent The pattern: contract terms and offtake explain more than sector labels Caution: bank-loan data from a consortium; the March 2020 study was not read Moody's Investors Service (2020), Default and recovery rates for project finance bank loans, 1983–2018: Sustainable project finance bank loans, Exhibit 2 (page 8) and pages 1–7. Total data sample of 7,354 projects.

title: Risk Falls with an Operating Record
text: Risk Falls with an Operating Record 19 Seasoning: default risk is highest in years 1 to 4 and falls steadily Convergence: by year 7 regions and uses of proceeds look alike, near single-A corporates Causes: market risk in Europe; country risk in emerging markets Entry point: buying a seasoned loan buys a lower-risk stage of the same asset Moody's Investors Service (2020), Default and recovery rates for project finance bank loans, 1983–2018, Exhibit 23 (page 25) and pages 1 and 7. Basel definition of default.

title: Blended Finance: Leverage Ratios
text: Blended Finance: Leverage Ratios 20 Overall: each US$1 of public commitment mobilised US$0.75 of private finance, 2013 to 2015 Low-income countries: US$0.37, rising to US$1.06 in lower-middle-income countries Infrastructure: the lowest ratios in low- and middle-income countries Reading: ‘billions to billions’ is more plausible than ‘billions to trillions’ Attridge, S. and Engen, L. (2019), Blended finance in the poorest countries: the need for a better approach, Overseas Development Institute, key findings (page 11) and pages 37–38. Nine selected MDBs and DFIs, 2013–2015.

title: Private Finance Follows Credit Ratings
text: Private Finance Follows Credit Ratings 21 Ratings: 96.3 per cent of mobilised private finance went to countries with a credit rating Default: country risk caused 36 to 46 per cent of emerging-market project defaults, and under 5 per cent in Europe Reading: instruments cannot supply the invdfestment climate Implication: enforceable contracts and priced risk come first Attridge, S. and Engen, L. (2019), ODI, pages 11 and 53; Moody's Investors Service (2020), page 7. Left panel: share of defaults caused mainly by country risk; EEA drawn at the bound of 5 per cent.

title: Megginson and Netter: The Survey Evidence
text: Megginson and Netter: The Survey Evidence 22 The claim: privately owned firms outperform state-owned firms, and privatisation improves operating and financial performance The scale: 75 of the Global 1000 were privatised firms in 1998; governments raised over US$500 billion in share offerings A welfare study: Galal and co-authors: gains in 11 of 12 divestitures, about 26 per cent of sales The condition: public ownership wins only where quality cannot be contracted and competition is weak Megginson, W. L. and Netter, J. M. (2001), From state to market: a survey of empirical studies on privatization, Journal of Economic Literature 39(2), 321–389; conference draft of December 1998, pages 2, 8–9 and 12–13 and the appendix summary table.

title: Two Readings of Private Provision
text: Two Readings of Private Provision 23 Megginson and Netter (2001), draft of December 1998, abstract and pages 12–13; Bel, Fageda and Warner (2009), IREA Working Paper 2009/23, abstract and pages 2–3 and 23. Journal version: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management (2010), not retrieved. Megginson and Netter Bel, Fageda and Warner Scope State-owned enterprises in many industries, mostly large firms Solid waste collection and water distribution Method Survey of before-and-after and comparative studies Meta-regression of 27 econometric studies Finding Private ownership improves performance No systematic cost saving from private production What reconciles them Competition and regulation accompany the gains Savings depend on competition, contract design and asset specificity
